morph.stmt: No source gives a one-line typological profile of Duau; from Lithgow's (1976) comparative charts Duau is mixed prefixing-suffixing in the usual Papuan Tip way: verbs take subject person prefixes (ya-, ku-, i-, ta-, ka-, wa-, si-; subjunctive da- between prefix and stem) and object person suffixes (-au/-gau, -o/-go, -ya, -da, -ma, -mi, -dži), aspect is by stem reduplication and 'I found no indicator of future tense in this family' (§68 p.470); nouns take inalienable possessor suffixes (-gu, -u, -na) with preposed possessive classifiers (kagu-/kana-, igu-/ina-) for the other possession classes, a definite suffix -ina and plural suffixes (-ho, -aho type), plus a comitative prefix ma-.

1069.prule: Two reachable primary grammars state different rules. van Driem 1993 (Baksila dialect): weak stress placed by morphological class -- verbs and deverbatives on the root, nouns and other parts of speech on the first syllable, affixes never stressed, unpredictable cases marked lexically. Rai 2016 (Makpa dialect): stress non-distinctive; monosyllables stressed; 'a great majority' of disyllables of all word classes (nouns, pronouns, adjectives, adverbs, verbs, infinitives) and trisyllables of all word classes take PENULTIMATE stress, with trisyllabic nouns shown stressed on the second syllable (sam'baki 'potato', bi'rʌsi 'chilli', bar'boti 'sweet yam'), which contradicts van Driem's noun-initial rule; nothing said about words of 4+ syllables. The two agree for most disyllables (noun initial = penult; verb root + suffix = penult) and that stress is weak/non-contrastive; they diverge for trisyllabic nouns and for suffixed trisyllabic verbs. The divergence may be dialectal (Baksila 1987 fieldwork vs Makpa 2013 fieldwork) rather than an error in either source.

1072.heavy: Long vowels (phonologically contrastive length, confined to non-initial syllables): 'Stress on long vowels in final closed syllable of a disyllabic word or in second syllable of a trisyllabic word'; summary: 'Stress lies on the long vowel in a non-final syllable or in a final closed syllable.' A word-final open-syllable long vowel is NOT stress-attracting (ḏína:, wúɽu: initial-stressed). Closed syllables with short vowels are not described as heavy.
1072.dflt: Initial stress in 2-3 syllable words (10, 100); first + penultimate in words of 4+ syllables (1010; sec. 2.4(iii) implies 10010 for 5 syllables, whereas the ch. 1 summary 'first and every alternate syllable, final unstressed' implies 10100); final syllable always unstressed.
1072.prule: Long (contrastively long) vowels attract stress: a long vowel in the final CLOSED syllable of a disyllable, or in the second syllable of a trisyllable, is stressed (gulá:y, wuɽú:ri-l, diná:la); a word-final long vowel in an OPEN syllable does not attract stress (ḏína: 'foot', wúɽu: 'river' are initial-stressed). With no such long vowel: initial stress in 2- and 3-syllable words; first and penultimate syllables stressed in words of 4+ syllables; the final syllable is never stressed. Ch. 1 summary restates the default as 'first and every alternate syllable, except that the final syllable must be unstressed'. Long vowels never occur in initial syllables of polysyllables, so all stated heavy-attraction cases are syllable 2.
1072.srule: Primary and secondary stress are not distinguished by Patz (1978). 2- and 3-syllable words carry one stress; words of more than 3 syllables carry two marked stresses, on the first and on the penultimate syllable (gáɲaráŋgu, dámaríŋgu, bírbi-birbí-la), neither ranked as the main stress. The ch. 1 summary words this default as 'the first and every alternate syllable, except that the final syllable must be unstressed', while sec. 2.4 says Dyabugay lacks Yidiny's strict S/U/S/U alternation and 'appears to favour a more loose S/U/U sequence'; 4-syllable words are marked first + third (gáɲaráŋgu, dámaríŋgu, bírbi-bírbi) and 5-syllable forms first + fourth, i.e. penultimate rather than alternate (bírbi-birbí-la, and the a-insertion verbs wábar-a-gáliŋ, wáŋgal-a-gáliŋ, ŋúndal-a-gáliŋ cited for the 'more loose S/U/U sequence'); words of 6+ syllables are not exemplified.

1074.tone: Diallo 2001 (Burkina Dioula orthography) presupposes lexical tones (tons hauts / bas), word tonal schemes (all-H, all-L, L..H, H..L), tonal compactness in compounds and a floating low tone marking the definite; it states no stress or word-accent rule (its 'accent aigu/grave' are orthographic tone marks). Bamba 1990 (Odienné Dyula; the accent paper A misattributed to Braconnier) gives the phonology: 'The underlying tones are L (low) and H (high)'; he reanalyses lexical H as an underlying accent ([s w] foot) and L as absence of accent, the definite being realised as an accent (superhigh) on the noun's final syllable, and notes 'In Odyene Dyula, it is not easy to distinguish H tone from accent'; his own conclusion calls it 'a metrical analysis of a tone language'. Accent placement in that analysis is lexical (= where H is), not computed from word position, so no word-stress rule exists under either the tonal (Braconnier 1982-83) or the metrical (Bamba) analysis. Delafosse 1929's weak, pitch-defined final 'accent tonique' for Mandingue as a whole predates tonal analysis and plausibly reflects final/definite pitch events.

tn.quote: Elle fournit des indications pour la notation des tons lexicaux et pour la notation d’un ton grammaticale qui en dioula signifie la substantif défini. … lorsque tous les tons d’un mot sont hauts, ce mot porte un accent aigu sur la première syllabe. … [fárá] … Lorsque tous les tons de mots sont bas ce mot ne porte aucun accent … kuru "boule" [kùrù] … Lorsque le mot comporte à la fois des tons hauts et bas selon un ordre décroissant en note tous les tons. … mámìnɛ̀ "fiançailles" [mámìnɛ̀] … le Diula connais un ton bas flottant qui s’associe à la base nominale pour signifier le défini.
tn.translation: It gives directions for writing the lexical tones and for writing a grammatical tone which in Dioula signals the definite noun. ... when all the tones of a word are high, the word bears an acute accent on the first syllable. ... [fárá] ... When all the tones of a word are low the word bears no accent ... kuru 'ball' [kùrù] ... When the word has both high and low tones in descending order all the tones are written. ... mámìnɛ̀ 'betrothal' ... Dioula has a floating low tone which associates with the nominal base to signify the definite.

1074.cfw: Every modern first-hand description of Dioula — Braconnier 1990 and Bamba 1990 for the Odienné variety, Coulibaly 1983 and 1990, Sanogo 1995, Keita 2001 and Diallo 2001 for the Burkina jula — analyses it as a two-tone language with no word stress, and the only dissent, Delafosse 1929's claim that Manding has no tones but a weak final pitch accent, is a pre-tonal survey of the whole Manding cluster that all later work supersedes.

1075.dq: While Dzongkha does not have phonological stress, long and short rhymes are analogous to stressed and unstressed syllables (in contrast to Balti for which vowel duration is a weak correlate of stress).
1075.dloc: ch.3 'Suprasegmentals: tone and breathiness', intro, p.69; also Part III word classes (lexical vs relational words), p.141; abstract, p.ii
1075.prule: No phonological stress (explicitly denied); prosodic contrasts are register (high/low pitch with breathiness/glottalization), an emerging level/falling melody contrast, and vowel length; the lexical word is the tonal domain and bound relational morphemes fall under its tone.
1075.srule: None (no word stress at all): 'Dzongkha does not have phonological stress' (Watters 2018:69); secondary or rhythmic stress is not mentioned anywhere in Watters 2018, ch.3 'Suprasegmentals: tone and breathiness' (pp.67-134) or the Part III intro (p.141).
1075.quote: In a recent study of Balti, (Caplow 2016) found fundamental frequency to be a strong correlate of contrastive stress, suggesting that the transphonologization of stress to tone is a pathway of tonogenesis. While Dzongkha does not have phonological stress, long and short rhymes are analogous to stressed and unstressed syllables (in contrast to Balti for which vowel duration is a weak correlate of stress). Perhaps what is seen here is a manifestation of the transphonologization of length to pitch: a contrast in the duration of the second syllable is manifest on the first syllable in elevated an…
1075.loc: ch.3 'Suprasegmentals: tone and breathiness', intro, p.69; also Part III word classes (lexical vs relational words), p.141; abstract, p.ii
1075.idn: Dzongkha (dzo), 'a Southern Tibetic language within the Central Bodish branch of Tibeto-Burman' (Abstract), the spoken form of the national language of Bhutan, mother tongue of the Ngalong of the main valleys of western Bhutan; the author refers to 'the speech variety of Dzongkha I studied' (p.6) without naming a…
1075.tone: Watters describes Dzongkha tone as incipient: a high/low register pitch contrast correlated with onset type (voiceless vs devoiced/breathy obstruents; plain vs glottalized sonorants), a level vs falling melody contrast in certain rhyme types (after Mazaudon and Michailovsky 1988), and pitch effects of rhyme length assimilated across disyllables; stress is explicitly said to be absent, with long vs short rhymes called merely 'analogous' to stressed/unstressed syllables. The one other use of 'stress' (p.141, relational words 'do not take stress') is a loose phrasing inside the phonological-word definition, immediately restated in terms of tone.

1076.dq: Gilbertson: 'In words containing more than one long vowel the last receives the stronger accent' / 'In the matter of accent, prefixes are treated as if they formed inseparable parts of the words to which they are attached'; Jahani & Korn 2009 sec. 2.2.1 'Word stress': 'essentially, the last heavy syllable of a word is stressed' (intonation treated separately in 2.2.2).

1076.heavy: 'All long vowels are accented'; 'Diphthongs are accented in the same way as long vowels'; 'Quiescent letters, letters not followed by a vowel, are accented' (closed syllables); 'letters under the sign shadda, are accented' (geminates). Jahani & Korn (for the Karachi system they equate it with): 'A heavy syllable is one which contains a long vowel or diphthong or a short vowel followed by more than one consonant.'
1076.dflt: initial: 'In the case of short vowels the first should be slightly accented' (three short vowels: 'first and third')
1076.prule: Word accent is weight-driven: every long vowel/diphthong is accented and, of several, the LAST long vowel takes the stronger (main) accent; closed syllables ('quiescent letters, letters not followed by a vowel') and geminates are also accented; in words with only short vowels the FIRST is (slightly) accented, and in three-short-vowel words accent falls on first and third. Jahani & Korn 2009 read this as 'essentially, the last heavy syllable of a word is stressed', i.e. the Karachi (Southern Balochi) type.
1076.srule: Gilbertson gives more than one accent per word (no term 'secondary'): all long vowels/diphthongs and closed or geminate syllables are 'accented', and of several long vowels 'the last receives the stronger accent', so non-final heavy syllables carry a weaker accent; in words of three short vowels 'the accent will generally fall on the first and third' (Korn 2003: 69-70 reads this as an additional accent on the final syllable when the first is accented: |saka|tar, |aska|nag). Jahani & Korn 2009 do not mention secondary stress for Eastern Balochi.

1077.dq: it is the stressed syllable of the suffix which bears the primary word stress
1077.heavy: No rime-weight criterion. The conditioning factor is the onset: 'the first syllable which is opened by a consonant' bears stress, so an onsetless word-initial V syllable is skipped.
1077.dflt: not applicable in rime terms; onsetless initial syllable -> stress on the second syllable
1077.prule: Stress is assigned to the first syllable opened by a consonant: consonant-initial words are stressed on the first syllable (neme [nə́mɐ]), vowel-initial words on the second (ineme [inə́mɐ]). Stated as a rule that 'covers a large number of lexemes', not as exceptionless.
1077.srule: Wilkins 1989 (section 2.2) gives no placement for secondary stress ('not entirely clear'). Henderson 2002: in words of four or more (VC) syllables, secondary stresses may occur on alternating syllables after the primary stress (atekertneme [ɐtə́kəʈɳə̀mə]~[ɐtə́kəʈɳəmə]); optional, more likely in citation forms.
1077.quote: 2.2 Stress. The assignment of stress (primary, secondary, clitics, etc.) in Mparntwe Arrernte is not entirely clear, and deserves fuller investigation. One rule that covers a large number of lexemes, is that stress is assigned to the first syllable which is opened by a consonant. morph.stmt: Exclusively suffixing (plus enclitics; no prefixes or proclitics): 'The first element in a verb is the verb root itself and the final element must be an inflectional suffix which indicates the dependency status of the verb' (§5.2 p.225; Figure 5-1: VERB ROOT + derivational suffixes + associated motion + continuous aspect + number agreement with S/A + reduplication + final inflection), and in the NP 'Case is suffixed to the final element of an NP and is the only slot which is obligatorily filled' (§3.1 p.102); Appendix 2 Part A is titled 'Suffixes and clitics'.

evidence_works.detail: States the same placement rule as the entry's Wilkins 1989 quote, in the same terms: 'In Arrernte, stress is assigned within a word to the first nucleus that is preceded by a consonant. Thus, if the word begins in a consonant, stress falls on the first vowel; if the word begins in a vowel, stress falls on the second nucleus (vowel) in that word.' (p. The refinement is analytic: the authors argue that surface consonant-initial words are underlyingly /e/-initial, so that 'stress in Arrernte falls on the second syllable and is computed at some level where the initial /e/ is present' (p. 3); the supporting argument is the plural/reciprocal allomorphy in (3)-(4), where consonant-initial monosyllables take the disyllabic-stem allomorphs (pp. 3-4), and section 3.1 (p. 11) restates that stress and allomorphy follow from underlying vowel-initial words. The article says it 'is based on Breen 1990' (unpublished; p. 1 note); the stress rule is given with four cited examples and no elicitation or measurement procedure, no instrumental data. It does not discuss secondary stress, the initial /a/ + /e/ variability, or suffix/clitic stress that Wilkins reports. Section 2.3 'Historical and Comparative Evidence' (p. 9; section 3 itself opens on p. 10) lists, paraphrasing Koch 1997, a historical change '10. Stress shift to second syllable' among twelve Arandic sound changes; p. 2 notes the utterance-final vowel 'may be stressed on occasion, as when it is the only vowel in the utterance'.

1080.prule: Reconstructed (from Coptic) word stress confined to a right-edge two-syllable window: conventionally ultima or penult (Peust's revised reconstruction: penult or antepenult, monosyllables aside); position within the window not predictable from the segmental string under the majority view (full vowel inventory in unstressed syllables), hence phonemic/lexical; stress position assumed constant from Paleo-Coptic through Coptic. Vowel quality/quantity of the stressed vowel is predicted FROM stress plus the number of following consonants (syllable structure rules), not the reverse.

1084.dq: Relative stress that is light/heavy occurs in every word. Two syllable words: Some stress is always on the first syllable.
1084.dloc: Hintze 1975 p.167 'The suprasegmental phonemes and their behavior: 1. Tone', p.168, pp.175-176 '3) Stress'; Lang 1973 pp. xvi-xvii; OPD 2004 p.2
1084.prule: Two-toneme (high/low) register tone system, lexically and morphologically placed (minimal pairs in Lang 1973/OPD; suffixes shift the marked toneme). Stress is explicitly non-contrastive and predictable from tone: 'Relatively heavy stress occurs only where there is high tone'; the main prominence therefore sits wherever the (lexical) first non-final marked/high toneme falls, not at a syllable-count or weight-defined position.
1084.srule: Light (non-primary) stresses, stated by the same source (Hintze 1975 pp.175-176): besides the heavy stress on the high-pitched syllable, light stress falls on syllables with upper-mid pitch (later non-final marked tonemes) and/or on the first and next-to-last syllables when these are two or more syllables away from the high and upper-mid syllables; in words whose single marked toneme is word-final (no heavy stress at all) light stress falls on the second syllable of trisyllables and on the first and next-to-last syllables of words of four or more syllables. Tone-conditioned plus edge (initial, penult) placement; no alternating count is described.

1084.exq_: Syllabic intensity or emphasis is semantically insignificant. Therefore, it is unmarked, since its occurrence is predictable.
1084.tone: Hintze 1975 (Mai Enga, primary): two tonemes, high and low, 'register type' system; pitch level carries the semantic load, length and loudness 'freely fluctuate' and are 'somewhat conditioned by pitch (high pitch induces loudness and/or length) and stress'. A separate 'Stress' section states stress is 'semantically insignificant', unmarked because predictable: heavy stress only on high-toned syllables, light stress elsewhere with positional defaults (first syllable; first and penult in long words whose only marked toneme is word-final). Word-level tone/stress is described separately from utterance-level pitch declination (p.168-169). Lang 1973 and OPD 2004 give only the two-toneme statement and minimal pairs (ámbí/ambí, ambáno/ambanó, tée/teé) and say nothing about stress. Nida & Osborne 1968 (Kyaka dialect, separate language) and Laycock n.d. remain unreached.

1086.dloc: Kap. II, § 39 'A. Den exspiratoriska akcenten', pp. 56-57; § 40 (musical accent); § 42 Anm. 3 (compound exceptions)
1086.prule: Main (expiratory) stress as a rule on the first syllable of the word, quantity-insensitive; loanwords (baron, kopek, parti, kvarter, butelj) also take initial stress. Exceptions only: some compounds (farm names, pronoun/adverb juxtapositions with weak first member, § 42 Anm. 3) and a few High-Swedish loans with unstressed prefixes be-/för-, which tend to drop the prefix as they nativize.
1086.srule: Simple words: none in Danell's description -- besides the initial main stress ('huvudton') simple words have only grades of weak stress ('svagton'; non-initial syllables are 'svagtoniga'). Strong secondary stress ('stark biton', nearly equal to the main stress) only in compounds: on the first syllable of the later member of a compound whose first member carries the main stress; in three-member compounds on the first syllable of the last member, the middle member unstressed. The High-Swedish loan suffixes -hait/-laik/-nigg/-skap may carry either svagton or stark biton.

evidence_works.detail: F0 contours (Praat/Simulekt) of 63 compounds from a 1965 Rickul-variety interview (Lagman and his mother) sorted into Lagman's four compound accent types, plus two read compounds from four elderly Rickul speakers (2009): simplex-accent compounds (Type 1, 3 tokens) carry one word-initial peak on the primary-stressed vowel and a fall, the secondary stress 'not phonetically realised' (p. 346); compound-accent compounds (Type 2, 31 tokens) show 'Like for Type 1' an early peak and a fall throughout the word, the hint of a second peak having 'turned out to be an artefact' (p. 347), summarised as 'single-peaked (one primary stress)' (p. 351); word-group-accent compounds carry two peaks aligned with the stressed syllables (p. 348); final-element-stress compounds (tole-sa 'such a', håla-mod 'in which way'; two tokens, 'extremely tentative') carry the peak on the second element (p. 348); contours resemble Finland Swedish, the no-accent-distinction variety (p. 349).

1088.prule: Tone language (each syllable carries its own lexical tone, up to five tones, unchanged in context). 1088.idn: Ewe (die Ewesprache): the Anlo-based written language with Interior (western inland) dialect forms; tone data mainly from the Interior dialects
1088.tone: Westermann 1907 sec. 51 (p. 37): 'Jede Silbe hat ihren eigenen Ton resp. ihre eigenen Töne, welche auch im Satzzusammenhang wesentlich unverändert bleiben. Die Silbe kann bis fünf verschiedene Töne haben und hat je nach ihrer Tonhöhe oder ihrer Tonzusammensetzung eine verschiedene Bedeutung.' Sec. 52 (body scan '53.', pp. 37-38): the tone of a syllable cannot be altered by rhythmic or other laws and stays the same in the sentence ('jedes Wort behält in jeder Verbindung den ihm eigentümlichen Ton'). Sec. 53 'Der dynamische Ton' (body scan '58.', p. 38): the only dynamic stress (Starkton) is a slight, physiologically explained strengthening of the first high tone of the sentence or compound word (or, absent a high tone, the first mid/low tone), so the sentence 'Hauptton' can fall on a semantically indifferent syllable simply because it is high-toned; sec. 54 lists syntactic substitutes (fronting, absolute pronoun, menye) for the missing emphatic stress.

1090.dq: For the prediction of placement of phonetic stress or stresses in a word, syllable weight is obviously most important phonologically. There is also the effect of intonation contours on at least the pitch, especially the final syllable, as apparently all or most intonation contours are falling.
1090.dloc: 2017 draft pp.120-123: Phonology > Prosody > 'Syllable definition and structure' (weight definition, p.120), 'Stress' (pp.120-122), 'Intonation' (opens p.122; the 'Eyak has stem-syllable stress... heavy-syllable stress' summary sentence is on p.123 within the discussion of Donlay 2009)
1090.heavy: Heavy syllables are all those that consist of more than CV, i.e. all syllables with full vowel (vowel with stigma, i.e.: tautosyllablic ’, or h), or syllables closed with one or more obstruents. (Light = 'open with reduced vowel'.)
1090.dflt: Not stated as a rule. Stems can never be light CV, so ordinary words always contain a heavy/stem syllable; for strings of reduced-vowel syllables Krauss only speculates about trochaic or iambic footing with contradictory examples (GAlA/XAlA/Xah vs ’ugAlA/XAde:/L).
1090.prule: Stress (impressionistic; no instrumental study) falls on every heavy syllable (any syllable more than CV: full vowel with: ' or h, or closed by obstruent) and on stem syllables, including the light first syllable of disyllabic stems; light open reduced-vowel CV syllables are otherwise unstressed. Non-culminative: a word may carry several stresses; the highest pitch peak tends to be the first stressed syllable, and when penult and final are both heavy the penult is higher (attributed to falling intonation). Possible trochaic/iambic footing in strings of equal-weight syllables is raised but left unresolved.
1090.srule: No separate secondary-stress category: stress is non-culminative, on every heavy syllable and every stem syllable, so a word may carry several stresses; the first stressed syllable takes the pitch peak of the falling intonation contour and later stressed syllables are progressively less prominent (final lowest). Alternating/footed rhythm in strings of equal-weight syllables is raised but 'by no means confirmed' (impressionistic, no instrumental study).

1092.heavy: full (vs reduced) vowel; syllable openness/closure also cited (a closed first syllable with an open and/or full-vowel second syllable favours 2nd-syllable stress in disyllables; closed full-vowel second syllable in polysyllables)
1092.dflt: initial (all vowels reduced, or all comparable -> word-initial stress; but 'either first or second' when both first and second are full in tri-syllables)
1092.prule: Dynamic (non-contrastive) word stress, default word-initial; shifts to the 2nd (occasionally 3rd) syllable when the initial vowel(s) are reduced and the later vowel is full (also conditioned by open/closed syllable shape); tri-syllables fluctuate; whole pattern stated as a prevailing/probabilistic tendency.
1092.srule: Polysyllabic words typically carry more than one stress, rarely on adjacent syllables: the stresses are separated by at least one or two syllables (1st+3rd, or 2nd+4th). The primary is most frequently the first stress in the word (1st or 2nd syllable); the secondary, 'or at least of an equal quantitative feature', follows it toward the word end (3rd, 4th, etc. syllable). Stated as typical, within an account the author calls a prevailing/probabilistic tendency.
1092.quote: Stress in Eastern Khanty is dynamic. In bi- or poly-syllabic words, the stress is often assigned to the word-initial syllable. Typically, if the first and the second syllables are comparable in vowel quality (all full, or all reduced) and syllable quality (all open, or all closed), stress appears on the word-initial syllable. The word-stress may also occasionally fall on the second syllable. This typically occurs in t…

1094.prule: No word stress, no lexical tone, no lexical pitch accent. Word-level pitch is purely intonational: an AP-level H tone docks at the right boundary of the first bimoraic foot of the Accentual Phrase, surfacing as an f0 peak on syllable 1 if heavy (long vowel/diphthong), else on syllable 2; IP-final disyllables peak on syllable 1 and the final syllable may reduce/devoice.
1094.quote: As for prosody, I find no convincing evidence for stress in Fataluku, although bimoraic feet play an important role in several aspects of the phonology. 1094.cfw: Heston 2015, the only instrumental study (four speakers, confirmed in Heston 2015 ICPhS and Heston & Locke 2016), finds no stress, tone or lexical pitch accent and shows that Campagnolo 1973's accent classes, reanalysed as lexical tone by Stoel 2008 for the South dialect, are really syllable-weight differences, but van Engelenhoven & Huber 2020 still call East Fataluku a pitch-accent language with predictable initial accent while granting that its word patterns match Heston's Central data, so the remaining disagreement is one of analysis rather than of observed fact. One further first-hand description conflicts (see the conflicting-description item); the entry follows Heston 2015.

evidence_works.detail: The article restates that Fataluku (Lospalos variety) has no convincing evidence for word stress and rejects earlier stress and lexical-tone analyses, so it agrees with the catalog's no-word-stress / no-tone entry. It adds that words are parsed into left-aligned bimoraic feet (shown by a two-mora minimal word, bimoraic reduplication and the absence of LH disyllables) and that the phrase-level rising-falling melody peaking on the second mora is an edge tone at the right edge of the first foot of each accentual phrase.
